title: UX Research Starts with Tasks
intro: The task is the atomic unit of usability testing. Get the task wrong, and even a perfectly run study produces misleading results. This article gives you a 3-step framework for writing tasks that reveal real behavior.

learn.title: Step 1: User goal, not UI action
learn.text:
Write tasks in terms of what the user is trying to **accomplish**, not what buttons to press.

❌ "Click on the Settings icon and find the notification preferences"
→ This tests whether they can follow instructions.

✅ "You're getting too many email notifications. Figure out how to reduce them."
→ This tests whether the interface supports the real goal.

try.q: Which task is correctly written as a user goal?
options: You need to add a new team member to your project. Set them up so they can start.
Click the 'Add Member' button in the top right and enter an email address.
Navigate to Settings > Team > Add Member.
Use the team management feature to invite someone.
try.explain: The first option frames a goal (add someone who can start working) without prescribing UI steps.

learn.title: Step 2: Realistic scenario
learn.text:
Wrap the task in a scenario that gives the user **context** and **motivation** — the same kind they'd have in real life.

❌ "Find a product under $50."
→ Why? For whom? What kind of product?

✅ "Your friend's birthday is next week. You want to find a gift for under $50 that they'd actually like. They're into cooking."
→ Now the user has a reason, constraints, and a way to evaluate success.

try.q: What does a realistic scenario add to a research task?
options: Context and motivation that mirror real-world use
More words to make the task seem professional
Constraints that make the task harder
Entertainment value for the participant
try.explain: Scenarios give users the same context and motivation they'd have in real life, producing realistic behavior.

learn.title: Step 3: No leading language
learn.text:
Don't use the same words the interface uses. If the button says "Manage Notifications," your task shouldn't say "manage your notifications."

**Leading language** tells users where to look, which means you're testing reading comprehension, not usability.

❌ "Use the **filter** feature to narrow results" (if the UI label says "Filter")
✅ "You only want to see items from the last month. How would you do that?"

The user should discover the path, not follow your breadcrumbs.

try.q: The UI has a button labeled "Export Report." Which task avoids leading language?
options: Your manager needs this data in a spreadsheet for a meeting tomorrow. How would you get it to her?
Use the Export Report button to download the data.
Export the report using the available tools.
Find the export functionality.
try.explain: It describes the goal without using UI labels. The user has to figure out that 'Export Report' is the path.

test.q: What are the 3 steps for writing good research tasks?
options: User goal, realistic scenario, no leading language
Clear instruction, time limit, success criteria
Simple wording, multiple choice, follow-up questions
Hypothesis, test plan, statistical analysis
test.explain: The 3-step framework: frame as a user goal, wrap in a realistic scenario, avoid leading language.

test.q: Why is "Click on Settings and find notification preferences" a bad task?
options: It tests instruction-following, not usability
It's too short
Settings is hard to find
It doesn't have a time limit
test.explain: Task prescribes UI steps. You're testing whether they can follow directions, not whether the interface works.

test.q: The button says "Archive." Your task says: "Archive the completed project." What's the problem?
options: Leading language — you're using the same word as the UI label
The task is too short
Archive is not a common word
Nothing — this is fine
test.explain: Using the UI label in the task tells users exactly where to look, defeating the purpose of the test.

test.q: A task reads: "Find a flight." What's missing?
options: A realistic scenario — where, when, why, for whom?
A time limit
Technical specifications
The correct answer
test.explain: Without scenario context, users have no motivation or constraints — their behavior won't match real-world use.

test.q: If you write tasks well but the interface is good, what should happen in the test?
options: Users complete tasks successfully — confirming the design works
Users fail — good tasks always expose problems
Users get confused by the scenario
Nothing useful — you wasted the study
test.explain: Well-written tasks reveal real behavior. If the design is good, success is the valid finding.
